Chan Master Zhongyan (Dharma heir of Chan Master Chang of Damei) and Master Damei Heshang (Dharma heir of Chan Master Chang of Guizong) ascended the hall and said:
"If you wish to recognize the Teacher of all Buddhas, recognize him within the mind of ignorance. If you wish to recognize the eternally abiding..."
The nature of carving. One recognizes it at the point where the myriad things undergo transformation. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Dame Mao?
The Master said, "The blade is not revealed. The monk asked, "Why is the blade not revealed? The Master said, "There is no one to meet it" (from the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*).

The Master of National Renown Liaowu was asked by a monk, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master held up his whisk. The monk said, "Is it not this very thing?
The Master lowered the whisk. He was asked, "It is not the character 'yi' (以), nor is it the character 'ba' (八). What character is it? The Master—
He drew a circle and showed it to him. There was a monk who drew a five-petaled flower within a circle before the Master;
the Master struck it through with his brush and drew another circle. This was Master Jiji (the Dharma heir of Chan Master Linji Xuan).
One day he addressed the assembly, saying: "It is not cold in winter; look after the year's end. He then descended from his seat.

A monk asked, "When racing horses compete for a ball, who is the one that gets it? The Master said, "Who is the one that does not get it?
The monk said, "In that case, it is not a matter of competing. The Master said, "Even to reach the point where there is no competition, there is still a fault.
The monk asked, "How can this fault be avoided? The Master said, "It has simply never been lost. The monk asked, "How is the state of 'not being lost' refined? The Master—
He said, "Held up by both hands, it cannot be lifted.
Wolong Heshang (the Dharma heir of Chan Master Yungai Yuan) asked, "What is the mark of a great man?
The Master said, "Within the purple silk curtain, he does not lower his hand. [The monk] asked, "Why is that?"
[The Master] did not dangle his hand. The Master said, "Not noble. Question: "In the midst of the twelve periods of the day, how should one apply the mind?
The Master said: "A monkey eating a fur-eating insect" (*Jingde Chuandeng Lu*).
Master Ruiyan (Dharma successor of Chan Master Gushan Zang) asked:
"When both black and white have perished and the Buddha-eye is opened, what then? The Master said: "I fear you will merely guard the interior.
He asked: "What is the Prince at Birth? The Master said: "He cannot be led out from the deep palace."
Master Boban asked, "What is Chan?
The Master said, "An ancient tomb is not one's home. He asked, "What is the Way? The Master said:
In vain are the tracks of carriage and horse. [A monk] asked, "What is the Teaching? The Master said, "The palm leaves cannot contain it all.
Daling Heshang (a successor of both Gushan Zang Chan Master and others).
A monk asked, "If one arrives at Tongguan Pass and then simply stops there, what then? The Master said, "That is merely the livelihood of the road."
[The questioner] asked, "What is the practical application within this? The Master said, "One may realize its essence, but one cannot embody it.
[The questioner] asked, "If one has realized its essence, why can one not embody it? The Master said, "Realizing the essence is a matter for what kind of person?
[The questioner] asked, "What is the matter within this? The Master said, "Do not act as if you were noble" (from the *Chuan deng lu*).
Chan Master Dawuwei (Dharma heir of Chan Master Xuefeng Cun) asked Yunzhu Wenheshang (Dharma heir of Chan Master Yunju Ying):
"What person can speak that which all Buddhas cannot speak? The Master said, "I, this old monk, can speak it. [The questioner] said, "All Buddhas..."
“I cannot say it. How would you say it, Preceptor? The Master said, “The Buddhas are my disciples. [The monk] said, “Please say it for me, Preceptor.
The Master said, “If one were not speaking before a sovereign, I would give him twenty blows. (From the *Chuan Deng Lu*)
Chan Master Qingyou and Chan Master Hui (both dharma heirs of Chan Master Yunju Ying);

There was the Prime Minister, Lord Pei Xiu, who convened a Dharma assembly and asked a monk who was reading a sutra, "What sutra is this?
The monk replied, "The *Sutra of the Silent Youth*. The Lord asked, "How many fascicles does it have? The monk said, "Two fascicles.
The Lord said, "Since it is 'silent,' why are there two fascicles? The monk had no reply. The Master spoke on his behalf: "If one discusses silence..."

National Preceptor Hye-gu of Do-bong Mountain (Dharma heir of National Preceptor Cheongyang Ui):
The Master first awakened to the fundamental principle in the chamber of Jeong-hye. The King of his own country, longing for him, dispatched an envoy to invite him.
He subsequently returned to his native land. The King received the secret instructions on the mind and treated him with ever-increasing honor. One day, he invited him into the royal palace. Above.
The Hall. The Master pointed to Weifenglou and addressed the assembly, saying, "Weifenglou has expounded the Dharma for you all, Venerable Elders.
Do you understand? If you do understand, how do you understand it? If you say you do not understand, why do you not understand Weifenglou?
Take care. The Master’s teachings had not yet spread throughout China; nor did they... [text ends].
Knowing his end, he passed away at the age of eighty-one. Gu-tam Hye-gam, State Preceptor, was surnamed Park;
he was the son of Jin-si Jeong-seung and a native of Beongjin-gun. He was born in the Jih-woo year (829). When the Master departed—
He was selected as the preeminent candidate among the nine mountains. King Chungnyeol ordered him to reside at Samjangsa Temple, where his disciples numbered seven hundred.
In the Jiwu year of the Yanhu period (1319), he fell ill. On the eve of his passing, a great tree on Mount Nam fell of its own accord, and a crimson vapor stretched across the valleys and mountains.
He was seventy-one years of age and fifty-eight years of ordination. The King bestowed upon him a posthumous title, and his stupa was named Gwangjo.

The Master was born into a Confucian family and entered the monastic order. From his youth, he was exceptionally intelligent and was able to exert himself diligently in his studies; as he grew older, he remained ever tireless.
Having achieved the highest rank in the selection for Mount Guryu, he cast off his robes and departed for Mount Kumgang. After completing his summer retreat, he moved his residence to Mount Jiri.

There, he did not indulge in rich flavors during times of hunger, nor did he don heavy furs against the cold; for many years, his side never touched his mat. Thus, while his physical traces remained hidden, his fame became widely renowned.
King Chungnyeol commanded him to reside at Samjangsa. His teacher, Master Caoxi Yuanwu, also exhorted him, whereupon he went.

Thereafter, he successively presided over monasteries such as Nangwe, Unheung, and Seonwon. All who received his instruction were like those who had been deaf and now heard, or like those who had been drunk and now awakened.
His disciples reached seven hundred in number, and many officials and scholars donned their robes to join the community.
They were beyond count. Yi Mengshan of Zhongwu saw his prose and verses and praised them incessantly, composing over ten matching poems in response.

He then sent a letter bestowing upon him the title "Gutan" (Ancient Abyss). In the Gui-chou year of the Huangqing era, the Grand Marshal Wang Yan, while residing at Yong'an Palace, sent a carriage and humble invitations to summon him to the capital.
At that time, eminent figures from both the Chan and doctrinal schools had gathered there daily.

They proceeded with the discourse in succession. The Master’s delivery was as vital as the whistling wind of the staff and shout, his eloquence flowing like a cascading river. The King was exceedingly delighted;

he traveled in the same carriage and personally presented him with offerings, bestowing upon him the dharma name "Venerable Wondrous Brightness, Patriarchal Master of the Separate Transmission, who Rekindles the Lamp of the Ancestors."

He first presented fifty ingots of silver as a parting gift for the master’s cassock, skirt, cap, and socks. Upon the master’s return to the mountain, he entrusted everything to the monastery’s permanent endowment (changzhu), returning nothing to his private possession.

He bathed and changed his robes. He composed a final letter and personally selected the site for his burial. Deep into the night, he summoned his attendant to strike the drum, donned his *kāṣāya*, and sat upon the meditation seat.
With a loud shout, he bid farewell, saying in brief: "The five aggregates are cleared away; true illumination is infinite."
Death and birth, emergence and submergence; the moon revolves in the void. Now that I have set foot down, who can discern my dark traces?

I tell you, my disciples: do not vainly feel about the empty sky. When the Chan practitioner Jinghu asked about the meaning of his "staying," he replied, "Where would there be a place where we do not meet?
Regarding such words as "crossing the river without using a raft," he struck his knee for a long time with his hand, smiled, and passed away.
Initially, his mother, Lady Zheng, dreamed that a celestial green curtain descended from the heavens. Upon it was a youth whose flesh and bones were like ice and jade;
as she looked at him, he joined his palms and leaped into her embrace. When she awoke, it felt as though a stone the size of a bushel had been placed within her womb.

Medical treatments and acupuncture proved ineffective, and on the sixth day of the eighth month of the Jǐyǒu year, the Master was born. Consequently, he was named Mù’ér (Curtain Child). He later manifested signs of passing away.
A man of Bandang-gun named Baek Tae dreamed that the Master ascended a green curtain and departed into the heavens.
Alarmed, he rushed to the temple the following day, only to find that the Master had already passed away (along with the preface to the stele composed by Yi Ch’i-hyon).
Honk’u (混丘): The Elder of Infinite Purity (Mugyeŭlŏn). His courtesy name was Kugyo (Kukki) and his pen-name was Kubyŏk.
His original name was Ch’ŏngbyŏn. He was of the Kim clan and the son of Kim Hongpu, who was posthumously granted the title of State Councilor (Kwŏnsaeng).

A native of Ch’ŏngp’ung County, he was born in the Sinhae year of King Chung-hon’s reign. Selected through the Nine Mountains (Kusan) examination, he was the first to pass the highest level (Ch’ŏngsa).
He abandoned his studies under Tu Pujo and pursued the learning of the Chan school. King Chungrye issued an imperial decree appointing him as Great Chan Master (Toedaeseun).

Upon King Deung’s accession to the throne, he was specially appointed as the Chief Monk Administrator (Dungsung) of the two monastic districts and granted the title of Grand Master (Daeseun). His son memorialized the court to enshrine the Master as the Royal Preceptor (Wangsa) of King Gwanji.
Both kings attended upon him in person to seek his instruction; consequently, he was ordered to reside at Yeongwonsa Temple. In the second year of Jiri, he moved [to another location].

He resided at Songlin Temple. He was seventy-three years of age and had sixty-three years of monastic seniority (*śramanera-varṣa*). He was posthumously granted the honorary title and temple name of Miaoying.

His works include two volumes of recorded sayings (*yulu*), two volumes of songs, eulogies, and miscellaneous writings, two volumes of a newly compiled ritual text for the *Shuilu* (Water-Land) ceremony, and thirty volumes of a recompiled collection titled *Zhishi yuyuan* (The Garden of Aids to Understanding).
In recent times, there was a great bhikṣu who elucidated the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to open up the school; he was named National Venerable Pujue.

His disciples numbered several hundred thousand, yet among them, it was only National Preceptor Baoguan who was able to penetrate the firmest points and draw from the deepest depths, achieving a wondrous resonance like that of the hen and chick pecking at the eggshell.
In his youth, he played with other children, gathering tiles and stones to build pagodas and temples; when resting, he would face a wall as if in deep contemplation.
His appearance was dignified and serene, and his nature was gentle and kind; thus, his relatives called him "Little Amitābha.

At the age of ten, he went to the Chan master Tianjing at Wuweisi to receive the tonsure. Selected from among the nine mountains, he was ranked first in the seventh category of examinations, yet he subsequently abandoned this path.

He studied under Pujue, vowing that he would not stop until he had personally perceived the innermost depths of the teaching. At first, Pujue dreamed of a monk coming to him who identified himself as Wuzu Faian.

The next morning, the Master went to pay his respects; Pujue felt privately strange about this. When the time came for the Master to sigh in admiration of his [the student's] agility and diligence, he said to the assembly, "My dream has been realized.
Subsequently, when he succeeded to the seat and opened the hall for formal preaching, his teacher and the assembly followed his regulations.
His demeanor was as composed and elegant as a finely executed painting, surpassing even that of Emperor Dezong.
When Dezong abdicated the throne, he resided at Yong'an Palace and repeatedly dispatched palace eunuchs to carry him there in a sedan chair; they conversed with ease upon the Way.

When evening arrived, he then informed the King that, according to the ancient precedents of his ancestors, the Master should be invested as the Royal Preceptor for the Contemplation of Wisdom, one who has perfected both realization and practice and awakened to the essence of the Buddha-mind.
The two kings rose from their seats and adjusted their robes to pay him honor—an act unprecedented since antiquity.

After several years, he requested retirement, which was granted. He was ordered to reside at Yeongwon-sa Temple. Originally a Chan monastery, it had come under the possession of the Chijja (Jich'e) school during the Yuanzhen era;
because of this master, it was finally restored to its former state.
While bathing, he preached the Dharma separately to the assembly, saying in brief: "Planting one's feet within a thicket of thorns;

concealing one's body amidst a forest of spears and halberds. Where, indeed, lies the path today? Where the white clouds are severed, there is the green mountain; yet the traveler stands even beyond the green mountain.
Having finished, he returned to his quarters, sat upon his bed, and passed away. The Master was profound and spoke little; he was a man of great learning.

There was nothing he did not examine. He was prolific in his poetry and prose. While traveling among the monastic communities, he encountered Chan Master Yi of Mount Meng in Wu, who had once composed the *Wuji Shuo* (Treatise on the Ultimateless) and sent it to him via a maritime vessel. The Master silently grasped the meaning of this and took for himself the title "The Elder of the Ultimateless."
Your servant has heard that the followers of the Buddha delight in speaking of cultivating one’s own person through merit and wisdom, for it is these that elicit a response from all things.

To be deficient in either of these two is insufficient for self-establishment; how then could such a person inspire confidence in others? Our Master was seven times promoted in rank and six times bestowed with honorary titles.
He visited nine renowned monasteries and twice resided in the Inner Court. As the head of the Buddhist community throughout the land, he received the two kings as his disciples.

Regarding these rites, no one has raised dissenting views; all have deemed them appropriate. Were it not for those who possess the dual adornment of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-saṃbhāra*), who could have accomplished such a thing?
By composing this inscription and carving it upon stone to transmit it to future generations, I, your subject, may be free from shame.
(Including the stele inscription composed by Yi Chi-hyeon.)
Hye-gin (惠勤), also known as the Lazy Old Man (懶翁), was posthumously titled Chan-gak (禪覺) and given the honorific name Pujŏ (普濟) Reverend.

His original secular name was Won-hye (元惠). He was a native of Nŭnghae-myo (寧海府) and belonged to the Ya (牙) clan by birth. He was the son of Yŏng-sui (令瑞), an official in the Bureau of Provisions (具膳官).
Her mother was Lady Zheng, a native of Lingshan Commandery. Zheng dreamed that a golden hawk flew in and pecked at her head;
suddenly, an egg fell from it, brilliantly colored with five hues, which entered her bosom. Consequently, she became pregnant and gave birth in the Gengshen year of the Yan’you era.
On the *gǐmǎo* day, he entered the mountains of the ninth month. He dispatched the inner attendant Jin Zhongsun to request his return.

On the *yǐsī* day of the third month, he went to the palace gate to petition for retirement; thus, his long-cherished vow was finally fulfilled. He traveled through Mount Longmen, Mount Yuanji, and other mountains.

On the *bǐwǔ* day, he entered Mount Jingang. On the *dìngwèi* day of autumn, he resided at Qingping Temple. That winter, he visited Baoyan Temple, where he took the hand of the monk Zhikong and donned his *kāṣāya*.
The Master wrote to his teacher, saying, "This is my final testament. In the year Jihyou (1309), he entered Taishan once more.

In the spring of Kengxu (1310), Sire Daeui brought the sacred remains of Jigong and interred them at Hwaeryam. The Master paid homage to the remains of his teacher and, in response to a summons, entered the summer retreat at Gwangmyeongsa.
At the beginning of autumn, he returned to Hwaeryam. In the ninth month, he began his practice at Gongboseon. This was the dwelling place of the Master.

The studio was named Gangweolhyeon (River Moon Pavilion). In the fifth month of the *bǐchén* year, he passed away while traveling in profound stillness; he was fifty-seven years of age and thirty-eight years of *dharmasaṃvatsara*.
In the ninth month of the autumn of the *gēngxū* year—the twentieth year of Emperor Hyeonryeong’s reign—the Master was summoned to the capital.

On the sixteenth day, [the Emperor] went to Guangming Temple, where the Master resided, and convened a great assembly of monks from the various mountains belonging to the two schools and five teachings to test what they had personally attained;
this was called the "Examination of Merit. His Majesty attended in person to observe it.
After the Master had offered incense, he ascended the Dharma seat and spoke, saying: "Break through the old molds of past and present; sweep away all distinctions between ordinary beings and sages."
This traces the origins [of the teaching] and severs the life-root of the monastics; it shakes off the net of doubt for sentient beings.

Mastery over its application lies in one's grasp; its transformative function lies in its timing. The Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations follow the same principle.
"Virtuous ones gathered here, please answer with truth. Thereupon, they entered the hall one by one to respond; bowing low and sweating profusely, they all said, "We have not yet understood."
Some were proficient in principle yet hindered by matters; others were so excessively deranged that they failed in their speech, retreating at a single phrase.

Although the Master’s countenance did not show any prior displeasure, when Master Ssu Chan of You-an arrived later, the Master questioned him on the three phrases and three barriers one after another.
After the meeting concluded, he returned to Huairan.
Reflecting upon Master Jikong’s prophecy regarding the three mountains and two waters, he wished to move his staff to Hwaegwan Hermitage.

However, as he was summoned to attend a Dharma assembly at this temple, he was granted permission to reside there. The Master said, "The late master Jikong once planned its reconstruction, yet it was destroyed by war.
How could I dare not continue his resolve? He then consulted with the assembly and expanded the halls and buildings. The work began.
When the announcement was completed, in the fourth month of the Bingchen year, a grand ceremony for the completion of the hall was held.

Master Heo considered that Hyegwan Hermitage was in close proximity to the capital, where men and women passed to and fro day and night in constant succession, leading to the neglect of their religious duties; he therefore petitioned to prohibit this.
Consequently, an imperial decree was issued to relocate him to Yeongwon-sa Temple. As he was being pressured to depart, the Master suddenly fell ill and was carried away on a litter.

He departed through the three gates and reached the edge of the pond. As he personally directed his palanquin bearers to exit through the Nirvāṇa Gate, the great assembly were all filled with doubt and wailed aloud.
The Master said, "Exert yourselves, my worthy attendants; do not let my sake cause you to stop midway.
My journey shall end at Liryeong. Upon reaching the Han River, he said to the escort official, Jol Cham, "I am ill..."

The journey was arduous. He requested to travel by boat upstream, arriving at Liryeong only after seven days. He further said to Jangok, "I wish to stay for a short while; I shall depart as soon as my illness subsides.
Jangok reluctantly complied with his request. He stayed at Sinleuk Temple. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, Jangok again urged him to travel quickly.
The Master said, "This will not be difficult; I am about to pass away. At the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. on that day, he passed away in silence.
He passed away. The people of the commandery looked up and saw a five-colored cloud-canopy over the mountain peak.
After his body had been cremated, rain fell without any preceding clouds over an area of several hundred paces. One hundred and fifty-five śarīra relics were obtained;

when these were prayed over and divided, they became five hundred and fifty-eight. Those among the fourfold assembly who obtained them from the ashes kept them for themselves, and no one else knew of them.
A divine light shone brilliantly for three days before it ceased. Śramaṇa Dali dreamed that a dragon coiled beneath the platform, its form resembling a horse.
When the funeral boat returned to Hwaeryam, there was no rain yet the waters rose; these were all attributed to the assistance of the Black Dragon.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, he enshrined the stūpa on the northern cliff of the temple, containing the cranial bone śarīra.
He was interred at Shenle Temple to demonstrate where his life ended. A stone bell was placed over him as a warning that no one should dare to tamper with the site.
This matter was reported to the court.
When he had just reached the age of twenty, a neighbor friend passed away. He questioned the elders, asking, "Where does one go after death? They all replied, "We do not know.
Deeply grieved in his heart, he went to Mount Gongde and sought ordination under Master Liao Ran. The Master asked, "For what purpose have you left the household life?
He replied, "To transcend the three realms and benefit all sentient beings; furthermore, I pray for your instruction. The Master said, "As for you—"
"Come here. What is this? He replied, "This is that which can speak, can hear, and can come; it is simply that it does not yet know the art of cultivation.
[The Master] said, "I am just like you; I also do not yet know it. You should go and seek it from other teachers.
In the Jia-shen year of the Zheng period, he went to Hwaeam Hermitage. Sitting alone day and night, he suddenly attained awakening while searching among the teachers.
The destiny of the nation was decided. On the *wùzǐ* day of the third month, he arrived at the capital of Yan. He consulted with Zhikong, and their responses were in perfect accord.
In the first month of the tenth year, the *gēngyīn* year, Zhikong assembled the multitude and posed a question; none were able to respond.

The Master stepped forward from the assembly and uttered several words, then performed three prostrations and withdrew. Zhikong was the one hundred and eighth patriarch of the Western Heaven. That spring, [the Master] traveled south to the Yangtze River.
Zhe. In the eighth month of autumn, he visited Pingshan. Pingshan asked, "Whom have you studied under? He replied, "Zhikong of the Western Heaven; I employ a thousand swords in my daily life.
Pingshan said, "Set aside Zhikong and his thousand swords for a moment; bring me your one sword. The Master took up his sitting cloth and brandished it at Pingshan.
Pingshan fell backward onto his meditation seat and cried out, "Thief! Kill me! The Master said, "My sword is capable."
"Killing a person can bring a person to life. He then helped him up. Seosan used the robe and whisk transmitted by Seonyang as tokens of his faith.
In the spring of the Sinmao year, he arrived at Mount Potalaka and paid homage to Avalokiteśvara. In the Renchen year, he went to Fulong Mountain to attend upon Qianyan.

At that time, over a thousand people from the rivers and lakes had gathered for the selection of those to enter the inner room. Qianyan asked the Master where he was from. The Master replied: [He recounted his journey].
Having answered, Yankong asked, "Before your parents were born, from where did you come? The Master replied, "This morning is the second day of the fourth month.
Yankong granted him permission. That year he returned north and once again attended Zhikong. Zhikong bestowed upon him a Dharma robe, a whisk, and Sanskrit scriptures.
Thereupon, he traveled through the mountains and rivers of Yan and Dai, remaining a solitary and carefree man of the Way.
His fame spread within the realm. In the autumn of the year Yiwei (1335), by imperial decree, he resided at Guangji Temple in Dadu.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month of the year Bingshen (1336), he established a formal opening ceremony for his hall (*kaifang fahui*).
The Emperor dispatched the Court Official Yexian Temür to bestow upon him a gilded cassock and silken fabrics; the Crown Prince likewise presented a gilded cassock and an ivory whisk.
The imperial robe arrived. The Master received the *kāṣāya* and asked the assembly, "The profound stillness of emptiness and quiescence is fundamentally without a single thing.
These brilliant and radiant forms—from where do they emerge? The assembly was speechless. He said slowly, "From within the golden mouth of the Ninefold Palace," and donned it.
He offered incense to pray for the Emperor’s longevity, ascended the seat, and with his staff held horizontally across his lap, spoke a few words and then descended. The year was Wuxu.

In the spring, he took his leave and pointed toward the sky; having received his prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), he returned to the East. Traveling and stopping as the occasion required, he preached the Dharma according to the capacities of his listeners.

After several days, their pleas became increasingly urgent. That evening, he dreamed of a divine being with a black mark upon his face. Together—

The next day, he went to the seat of the local deity and beheld its countenance; it was exactly as he had seen in his dream. Consequently, the bandits did not arrive.

Throughout his life, he had never practiced secular writing. Whenever someone requested that he compose a poem or inscription, he would take up his brush and write immediately, as if without deliberate effort;

It is only fitting that he was so versatile and capable (from the "Epitaph for Seonjak," composed by Yi Saek).

As for Neunong: his mother dreamed of a golden hawk flying in and pecking at her head; suddenly, an egg fell from it, resplendent with five colors, which she took into her bosom and thereby became pregnant (giving birth to Seon).

The tomb door opened of its own accord, and Master Zhigong emerged to preach the Dharma for them, transmitting his robes and alms bowl.
He further presented them with a python-skin sandal, entrusting them with these words: "To the west of Mount Niutou in your kingdom, there is a place where the Dharma Buddha shall flourish greatly.

Upon your return to your country, you should establish a separate monastery to supplement the great *saṃghārāma* Haiyin. Having finished speaking, he re-entered [the tomb]. Thus did the two masters [part ways].
Upon returning to their country, they reached Mount Ox-head (Gokuraku-zan). From the northeast, they crossed the ridge and proceeded westward.
Encountering some hunters, they asked, "As you range this mountain in search of game, do you know of any site suitable for founding a monastery?
The hunters replied, "A short distance below here, there is a marshy pool where iron tiles are abundant; you should go and inspect it. The two masters arrived there.
He saw him at a marshy pool; it was most agreeable to his intention. He sat upon the grass and entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Light radiated from the crown of his head, and a purple vapor surged toward the heavens. At that time, King Aejang, the thirty-ninth ruler of Silla, suffered from a carbuncle on his back.
Despite the efforts of skilled physicians, no cure was found, and the king was deeply distressed. He dispatched envoys in various directions, hoping to find a master physician.

"His virtue is extraordinary; perhaps he would deign to grant us aid. While on the road, the imperial messenger caught sight of purple vapors and suspected the presence of a man of异道 (extraordinary character).

After lingering there for a long time, he suddenly saw a fox climbing up the rock and departing. The messenger’s heart—
He found this strange. Following behind them, he saw the two masters enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*), whereupon light issued from the crown of their heads.

Filled with reverence and faith, he prostrated himself and invited them to return to the royal palace. The two masters did not grant permission. Thereupon, the imperial messenger informed them of the Queen’s affliction with carbuncles on her back.
The masters gave him five-colored threads and asked, "What object is there before the palace? He replied: [The rest of the text follows the narrative of the healing.]

The King was moved by this and revered it; he ordered the people of the state to establish this temple.
This was the third year of King Aejang (the Renwu year), according to the ancient records of Haerin Temple.
In praise of his virtuous conduct: The Great Master protects the East; the Youth travels the South. His body is a single cloud; his resolve is a thousand-li stream.

He received the imperial decree for the Dharma-seat like the Venerable Buddhabhadra; the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) hung from the ox-head peak; the elephant’s net [of wisdom] probed the profound mysteries. He chose the finest sites for his mountain retreats, reaching even to the seacoast.
The land is exalted with islands and peninsulas; heaven bestows forests and springs. The "Transformation City" is but empty talk; the "Scholar’s Thicket" is transmitted through the mind.
Her reflection is like the autumn moon; our feelings are separated by spring mist. She blooms as a lotus from amidst the flames.

Emperor Taizu fought against the Prince of Baekje, Mugwang. Mugwang relied on the Beomsong Mountain for protection;

The soldiers were terrified and subsequently surrendered. Thereupon, Emperor Taizu honored and served him with reverence, granting him five hundred *gye* of additional land and restoring his former [estate] (according to the ancient records of Haeinsa Temple).
In front of the bell tower of Songgwangsa Temple, there was a water pavilion where Great Master Pujō once stood. Before it grew a tree. When Great Master Pujō was approaching his passing, he said:
"After I am gone, this tree will surely wither. If it should sprout branches and leaves again, you will know that I have been reborn."
This year, though the tree reached a thousand years of age, it produced no branches or leaves. When people scraped away the bark with knives, the inner wood was moist and brimming with vitality.
Had it truly been dead, it would surely have withered and fallen; yet to this day, it remains as upright as ever (*Che-ri-jì*).
The ancestral master’s Jingeum (Golden Mountain) was originally a dragon pool; its depth was unfathomable and it lay to the south of Moak Mountain.

During the Silla period, the ancestral master filled it with tens of thousands of loads of salt until the dragon moved away. He then constructed a foundation and built a great hall, with steps at each of the four corners of the hall. It is very small.
Surrounded by mountain torrents, its pavilions and towers remain magnificent and its grottoes deep and profound even to this day;

In the autumn of the year Wuseung (758) of the Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, he was summoned to collect taxes.
The King’s grandfather was returning home from a village at dusk when he found a puppy on the road; it had three eyes. He took it home and raised it.
This dog was far beyond the ordinary breed: its form was like that of a lion and its nature was like that of a sage.
It ate but once a day and served its master with great diligence; it would go five *li* to meet him upon his arrival and escort him back when he departed.
For five *li*, he attended upon him on his return. From this time on, he loved and cherished him; he stroked him and comforted him.
When the third year, the *jiǎzǐ* cycle, arrived in autumn, the dog died while sitting peacefully without illness.
Juren prepared the coffin to arrange the funeral and prepared offerings for the sacrifice, as if mourning for a domestic pig. In the tenth month of winter in the *bǐngyín* year, Juren also...
As he was about to die, he first arrived at the gate and beheld a king. His face had three eyes, and his head was crowned with five peaks.
He held a precious scepter in his hand and wore crimson robes; his lips were like vermilion in motion, and his teeth were as even as white shells.
He sat loftily upon a jeweled couch, surrounded by attendants and officials all wearing black caps and red garments—ox-headed executioners and horse-faced rākṣasas—who stood in a dense, solemn guard.
The arrangement was like that of a world-king performing a public rite. When he saw that [the host] was abiding in benevolence, the king descended from the hall, took his hand, and said:
"Alas, O host! How could you have come to such a state? Recently, I was subject to a divine judgment;

"I have restrained myself. Now that you have suddenly come to visit me, how could I dare forget your virtue? He assisted him by leading him up the steps.
Only then did Ju Ren realize the reason for this, and he wiped away his tears, saying, "I am but a lowly man, naturally unlearned and ignorant.
How shall I be able to offer a formal plea when summoned to the underworld? I prostrate myself, praying that Your Majesty will grant me instruction and bring me joy. The King said, "Excellent."
"O benevolent one! Listen attentively to my words. To serve the Sages of the Netherworld, you must first bow your head and obey my instructions;
only then shall you follow me into the realm of Yama. When they arrived, King Yama asked, "While you were among the living, what causes and conditions did you create?
He replied, "Since my youth, I have served as an official's messenger and had no leisure to cultivate goodness. I was about to perform a great deed..."
Upon receiving these instructions, he returned to his celestial realm, forever sighing with regret in his heart. The King said, "Bring Ju Ren before me.
Ju Ren approached and took his place beneath the throne. The King asked, "What is it you desire that has not yet been fulfilled? Speak candidly. Ju Ren replied:
This humble servant has humbly heard that the Dharma-treasure is most precious, and he wished to carve it onto printing blocks to proclaim it far and wide; yet he has not been able to do so.
Merely possessing this aspiration, he has ultimately lacked the means to realize it, and for this reason he was filled with distress and fear. The Great King, bowing from his courtyard, said:
"I wish for you to ascend to the palace and rest there for a time. Ju Ren firmly declined, whereupon the Great King immediately commanded his officials to remove the name [from the register].

The Ghost Register (Guǐlù). Accompanied by his subordinates, he walked outside the gate, where he consoled them and saw them off with a bow. After Jūren retired, he went to the residence of the King of Sānmù.
The King had already ordered a seat to be prepared in anticipation and invited him to sit. They conversed with refined grace, and the King repeatedly cautioned and instructed him, saying:
"My lord, do not worry at all about the magnitude of the matter. Upon returning home, purchase paper and proceed to..."

He went straight to the gate, where the usher entered to announce him. The Princess said, "Welcome, O transformed monk.
Have you encountered no further hardships on your journey? I am the Ghost King of the Three Eyes. I have made an appointment with you, which is why I have come here. She spoke again.
The king said, "This man recently entered the realm of the dead, where he was exhorted to return to the world of the living.
Those who carve the scriptures for circulation wish for the King to act as a great donor (*mahādānapati*) to assist in accomplishing this great task. What do you think?

If it be so, not only will the Princess be free from harm, but the sovereignty of the state shall be eternally secure, and Your Majesty shall also enjoy long life. The king bowed and replied, "So be it."
Thereafter, she remained with Juren (Residing Benevolence) for a while; showing a manner of regretting their parting, she manifested her form and departed.
Princesses and others regained their original minds, immediately rose, and prostrated themselves before their father, the King, and mother, the Queen, saying:

"It would be well to perform virtuous deeds even in the realm of the dead, let alone in the benevolent kingdom of the living world. Parents, do not neglect this! The King replied, "So be it. Thereupon—
He treated the master of the ordination ceremony with great kindness, exhausting his private savings to provide for him.
He issued orders to both the inner and outer households to assemble skilled artisans on Gijeo Island to embroider the sutras upon paulownia wood, which were then gilded and lacquered.

These were transported to Haeminsa Temple on Mount Gaya, where he established a ritual assembly for the Twelvefold Praise (Sulchido-jan). All of this was brought about by the unseen powers of the underworld.
This was truly not the private whim of the King of Ghosts. The husband and wife of Jurén attained longevity, health, and tranquility, and both ascended to the Land of Bliss.
Alas! It is clear that the Yang-fa is a treasure; there is nowhere it is not treasured. Why is this?
Because the King of the Netherworld treasures it and thereby governs the realm of the dead with excellence, while the Ruler of Men treasures it and thereby fully attains the hearts of the people.
The Celestial King treasures it and enjoys longevity and happiness; the Awakened Sovereign treasures it and bestows benevolence upon the myriad species.
Such explanations are recorded in the postscript to the Tripitaka (by Imperial Envoy Mao Guoqi).

however, King Sunmyeong immediately ordered his release, saying, "I grant him my own paintings and poems," and permitted him to return to the mountain. In the Year of the Water Dragon (1592)...

During this period of turmoil, the Master took up his sword and proceeded to the imperial encampment, where he was granted an imperial decree appointing him as the General Superintendent of the Eight Provinces.
The Master led his disciples, dividing the monks to assist the royal troops. They advanced into battle and inflicted heavy casualties.

Subsequently, they escorted the Emperor back to the capital, where the Master requested to return to his former residence; King Sunjo granted his request and bestowed upon him the title Gukil-do (National First Rank).

The Great Chan Master, who universally encompassed both Chan and the Teachings, supported the school and upheld the doctrine, and was a Venerable One who brought all beings to the stages of liberation, entered parinirvāṇa at Miaoxiang Yuanjian Monastery in the year Jiachen (1504). He was eighty-five years of age, with sixty-five years of Chan ordination seniority.

His writings include *Chanjia Guijian* (A Mirror for the Chan School), *Chanjiao Shiyunshuitan* (The Cloud-Water Altar of Chan and Teaching), and *Sanjia Yizhi* (The Single Finger of the Three Schools), each consisting of one fascicle. [Recorded by] Qing.
The *Hutang ji* (Collected Works from the Empty Hall) in eight volumes was published; it is said that his calligraphy is sparse yet forceful and full of character.
He offered sacrifices at the Myo-hyang Chongjik Shrine and the Pyochong Shrine in Milyang.

Wen Zhiqin said: "The worldly and world-transcending dharmas do not contradict one another, whether external or internal. Since ancient times, among the venerable elders of the Empty Gate (Buddhism), there have been few who exerted their efforts in the affairs of state.

Assisting in the heavenly retribution, he overcame [the rebels] with valor; the brilliance of his restoration was renowned throughout both China and the barbarian lands.

Yet, as for my Master’s mind, how could it ever have engaged in any deliberate action? He manifested traces in accordance with conditions, yet his efficacy was preeminent; his mind remained poised between emptiness and existence.
Yet his deeds have brought glory to loyalty and righteousness; I venture to rely on this to make my earnest request.
His mother, Lady Jin, had a miraculous dream while pregnant with him. When he was three years old, an old man suddenly appeared and said, "I have come specifically to seek a young śramaṇa.
He then took the boy, chanted several incantations, and rubbed the child's crown, saying, "He should be named Yunhe (Cloud Crane). Thus it was said.

Having finished, he departed through the gate, and no one knew where he had gone. In his childhood, his play was invariably centered on Buddhist rites. As he grew slightly older, his character and spirit were exceptionally brilliant;
his speech startled those who heard it, and he was beloved by the provincial governor, who hailed him as a "prodigious child.

At the age of ten, [his mother] petitioned that she was left alone and destitute with no one to rely upon; the governor took him to the capital to study at the Confucian college (the *pan*). Whenever he sat for examinations, he immediately...
Feeling dejected and frustrated by his lack of success, he traveled south into the T’ou-liu region to explore the wonders of its cliffs and caves.

There, he perused the Buddhist scriptures extensively and suddenly conceived the aspiration for world-transcendence. Taking leave of his companions, he composed a poem which says: "Returning from drawing water, I suddenly turned my head back;
Countless green mountains lie amidst white clouds. He then went to the Elder Ch'ung-jin to shave his hair and become a monk. Following him...
In the year Jiajing Gengzi, when the Master was twenty-one years old, the Chan Master Yichan received the full precepts.

He subsequently visited Master Lingguan and attained his seal of approval (*kanna*). Later, while traveling through the villages, he suddenly attained realization upon hearing the crowing of a cock at noon.
He sighed and said: "I would rather be a simpleton for a lifetime than become a pedantic monk of the books. He then took up [his staff].
He inscribed a verse upon a fallen leaf, saying: "The hair has turned white, yet the heart remains unrefined; this was leaked by the ancients.

Now, hearing the cry of a single cock, the task of the dog-man is complete. Thereafter, he traveled on cloud-like journeys through the various famous mountains of Guandong. By chance, he entered the capital.
He passed the examinations for the Chan (Seon) curriculum and was promoted to serve as an adjudicator for both the Chan and doctrinal schools.

Before long, he cast off his robes and entered Mount Pongak, where he composed the "Three Dreams Poems. A certain Chan master, on the verge of death, had uttered a prophecy: "A single robe has debts; a wooden man contends for green;
it is not that there are no legs, but they come from the Southern Ocean. When Master [Sugwang] arrived at this mountain, he prayed for the enshrinement of the śarīra relics.
His spiritual responses were manifest and brilliant. Although the Master concealed his traces and obscured his brilliance, his reputation for the Way grew ever more exalted;
those who were vain, arrogant, and conceited were intoxicated by his fame upon merely hearing of him and vied with one another to pay him homage from the north.
In the year Jichu (1579), the "Rebellion Case" broke out; falsely accused by a demonic monk, he was arrested. During his interrogation in prison, he spoke with clarity and eloquence.
King Seonjo, who had long heard of his reputation, immediately ordered his release. He was summoned for an audience and granted an imperial composition and a hand-painted bamboo screen.
The Master composed a poem on the spot to express his gratitude, which further won the King’s praise. He was then provided with generous gifts and returned to the mountain.
During the disturbances of the Incheon era (1482), King Seonjo fled to the west. The Master went out from the mountains to pay his respects at the imperial camp.
The King said, "The nation faces a great calamity; how can a mountain recluse remain at ease? The Master wiped away his tears and replied that he was willing to offer his life in service.
The Emperor praised him and issued an edict appointing him as the General Superintendent of the Chan Teachings for Entering the Way.
The Master then commanded his senior disciples to rally the assembly of followers. Thereupon, Wuijeung rose up from Guandong and Chueo-yeong rose up from Hunan;

Accompanied by several hundred attendants, he escorted the imperial carriage back to the capital. He addressed the Sovereign, saying, "I am old and approaching death;

Intending to pass away at Wonjigam Hermitage, he traveled by palanquin through the snow on that day to visit various nearby mountains. He paid homage to the Buddhas and preached the Dharma;
