An anthill; a thousand households where the wealthy treat men like minced chicken. A bright moon through a single window, its clarity resting upon the pillow. The infinite pine winds, their melodies never the same.
Therein lies the intent of one who transcends the mundane world, looking down upon the dusty realm from beyond—it was composed as a momentary realization (from the *Xiyā jí*).

Wizung (Vijaya): After the壬辰 (Injin) upheaval, Master Songun Hongji served as a general of the righteous monks (*uisaeng*) on the battlefronts of the southern peninsula. There, he was summoned by the Japanese general Kiyomasa to meet with him.
Matsunaga Munemori entered the Wada camp. The bandits stood in formation for several *ri*, their spears and swords packed like bundles.
Munemori showed no sign of fear; seeing Kiyomasa calmly conversing and laughing, Kiyomasa said to him, "Does your noble country possess any treasures?
Munemori replied, "Our country has no other treasure; we regard only your head as a treasure. Kiyomasa asked, "What do you mean by that?"
He replied, "My country will purchase your head for a thousand catties of gold and ten thousand households of a fief; what treasure is there that it would not value? Jeongseong laughed loudly.

Since the Imjin War (1592), the Japanese had not dared to seek peaceful relations; it was not until the Gui-mao year (1623) that they sent an envoy to request a diplomatic mission, which filled everyone with indignation.
I lamented this. The court, fearing that he might cause further unrest, dispatched a mountain man to test the sentiments of the rebels.

The mountain man circulated various petitions among the high officials. I presented him with a verse, saying: "In this age of prosperity, many are renowned generals; Yet peerless merit belongs to you alone, O Master. Your boat sailed upon the sea of Lu Lian;
Your tongue was employed in the eloquence of Lu Sheng. The barbarians’ deceit and guile know no satiety; The task of binding them remains."
Fearing for his life, he had a long sword at his waist. "Today I am ashamed to be called a man" (from *Jipyeong yuseso*).
In the *Renchen* year of the Wanli era, while residing at Yudam-sa on Mount Geumgang, a great force of Japanese troops arrived.
Together with a fellow monk, he took refuge in a deep valley. Another monk went out to scout; the Japanese entered Yudam-sa and bound dozens of resident monks.
They demanded gold, silver, and various treasures; when [the monk] would not produce them, they were about to kill him. When Fayong heard of this, he wished to go and rescue him.
The monks all pulled him back, saying, "If our teacher wishes to save a fellow monk from death, his compassion would be unsurpassed."
However, to reach into a tiger’s mouth and grasp its whiskers is of no benefit; it only brings disaster. Yet Zheng did not heed this advice.

He entered the midst of the chaotic troops as if there were no one beside him. The Japanese soldiers found his behavior strange. When they reached Shamon, some of the Japanese were sitting while others were lying down.
Swords and halberds were clashing and forging; thus, he did not bow or salute, nor did he look back or linger in his steps.

Dragging his staff and waving his hand, he entered. The Japanese observed him closely but did not restrain him. He passed through the Shadow Pavilion of the Mountain and arrived beneath the Dharma Hall.
All the monks were bound in the two corridors; upon seeing Weizheng, they wept, but Weizheng paid them no heed. There was a Japanese man in the Zen hall.
Regarding the external documents, such as the military registers: the official Zhengli (Zheng) looked at them, yet the Japanese soldiers did not even restrain themselves from shouting.
Observing that the characters were unintelligible, he went straight up to the Dharma Hall. There, all the Japanese generals sat in a row upon chairs;
only Zheng mounted his hand [the platform] without performing a formal greeting. He wandered about, gazing at them like a madman. One general took the document...
He asked, "Do you understand written characters? Weizheng replied, "I have a rudimentary understanding of them. He asked again, "Does your country honor seven patriarchs?

Weizheng said, "There are six patriarchs; how could there be seven? [The Japanese official] said, "I wish to hear about them," whereupon Weizheng set down the names of the six patriarchs in writing for him to see.
The Japanese general was greatly amazed and remarked, "This temple possesses gold, silver, and various treasures."
"You must bring them all out; otherwise, I shall have you executed. Wei Zheng said, "In our country, we do not treasure gold or silver;

we use only grain and cloth. Gold, silver, and various precious gems are rare throughout the entire nation, let alone for a mountain monk who serves only to make offerings to the Buddha, eating vegetables and wearing grass garments, sometimes fasting from grain to eat pine needles, or begging for food among the village lanes."
How could one who has been born [into this world] ever hoard treasures such as gold and silver? This morning I observed that you, General, are capable of understanding Buddhist matters.
The Dharma of the Sixth Patriarch holds compassion and non-killing as its supreme principle. Now I see an innocent, simple monk bound beneath the eaves and interrogated for precious goods.
That man carries but a single staff and a thousand miles of robes, seeking alms among the common people to sustain himself from day to day.

"Though one were to cut the flesh from one's body or grind one's bones to powder, how could there be even an inch of treasure? I pray that the General will spare him. When the various Japanese officials circulated this letter, their expressions changed with emotion;
they looked down at their subordinates and spoke. The subordinates hurried down to the hall and released all the more than twenty monks from the two corridors.
At this, Wéizhèng again waved his sleeve and, leaning on his staff, walked out. The Japanese general then wrote in large characters: [The text provided ends here.]
A notice was posted, stating: "This temple houses a high monk who knows the Way; let no soldiers enter further. Thereupon, the troops withdrew.
From then on, the Japanese soldiers never again entered Yudian Temple. The imperial court subsequently appointed the monk as a military commander.

He led a monastic army into battle, moving in and out of the Japanese ranks with the mission of conducting diplomatic persuasion. Once, while entering the enemy lines, he encountered the Japanese general Kiyomasa.
Kiyomasa asked, "What is the most precious treasure in your country? Weyi Zheng replied, "In our country there is nothing precious;
the only thing we hold as a treasure is the head of the General. Kiyomasa forced a laugh, yet in his heart he was truly intimidated.
Once the rebellion was quelled, he received an imperial decree to enter the country of Japan. Tokugawa Ieyasu gave him twenty thousand *kin* of cotton cloth (*unmen*), but he declined it;
unable to refuse, he gave it all to the Lord of Tsushima, Tachibana Chishō, and returned home.
Later, when the Imperial Court renovated the ancestral shrines and palaces, he mobilized the monastic forces of the entire province to assist with the labor (from the *Uonodan*).

During the disturbances of the *Injin* (1592–1598), he championed the righteous cause against the Japanese invaders and captured vast numbers of enemy troops. Consequently, His Majesty specially appointed him as a Great General of the Sangha;
his fame filled both countries. After the disturbances were quelled, Yon Kōkaku became the Shogun (*Kankoku*) of Japan and requested an envoy from our court.
While the people were all indignant and lamented this, the Imperial Court feared the outbreak of border hostilities and sent Yuil Chong (Wijeong) to Japan.
This was done to test the intentions of the enemy. The Japanese had long revered his reputation and, wishing to test his integrity, threatened him to force him to surrender.
Chong said, "I have received my mandate from my King to serve as an envoy to a neighboring state; it is not fitting for you to act with such aggression.
My knees shall not bend before you. The Japanese then again fanned a charcoal fire until it blazed like a red furnace and ordered Chong to throw himself into it.

He entered into the midst of the fire, yet his countenance remained entirely unmoved. As he stood by the side of the flames, just as those who were about to leap in, the heavens suddenly sent down rain that poured like a torrent, and the fire was instantly extinguished of its own accord. The Japanese, beholding this, regarded him as divine; they then prostrated themselves in worship, saying, "The protection of Heaven is such as this;
the Great Master is truly a living Buddha. They immediately carried him away in a golden palanquin. From that time on, even though...

Whenever he visited the privy, he would invariably carry the painting there to attend to it. He would report his arrival and inquire after the Great Master’s wishes, saying, "I shall certainly honor your commands;
please tell me what you desire. Zenpō replied, "I, a mountain man, have no desires at all. I only wish for my country to return one scroll of Buddhist painting.
The Shogun said, "Although our country is small, we still possess many treasures. Why would you discard this to take that? Zenpō—
He said, "This Buddha is most efficacious; one may pray for wind and rain through it, and one may ward off calamities and bring about auspiciousness.
Therefore, I wish to have it returned. The Grand Councillor and those below him spoke with one voice, saying, "The Great Master can also summon the wind and call forth the rain;
why must you seek the return of the Buddha image? Consequently, they did not force its return. From that time on, the Japanese were not dared to do so again.
"Hai! To this day, I have sought out the calligraphic works of Songyun and would certainly purchase them at a high price, fearing only that I might lose them.
At Mount Bagong in Daqiu, there was once a Daoist who bought eight rolls of fine silk in the marketplace of Yan and joined them together into one.
[He] desired to paint a sixteen-foot golden body as a hanging scroll (*paṭa*), traveling through the eight directions to widely recruit a capable painter. After several years, he had not found one.
It happened that the monk Da-jang of Mount Kumgang was holding a *shuilu* (water-land) assembly, where monks and laypeople had all gathered, numbering no fewer than several thousand.
The presiding monk (*huazhu*) announced his request to the great assembly, wishing to obtain a hand for painting the Buddha, but there was no one who responded. He sat [there].
An elderly, infirm monk responded to the call and went with him back home. After purifying himself through ritual bathing and fasting, he made his request.
The monk said, "This matter will be accomplished in thirty days. I shall remain within the Buddha hall, concealing my body to perform it. Be careful not to peek.
Seal the four walls so that there are no gaps or openings, leaving only a single hole for offering rice. Three days passed.
He took one coin. As he took it, he also refrained from looking askance. The presiding monk, fearing a transgression, did not dare to look at him as he had instructed.
On the twenty-ninth day, [the master] calculated that although it was not yet a full day, the painting must surely be finished. He cast a fleeting glance to look at it;
the painter was greatly startled, threw down his brush, stood up, and said, "The painting is not finished. Immediately, there appeared a yellow magpie.

It emerged from the bowl and flew away; its trace was silent and still. The presiding monk, finding this strange, entered to look and saw that the painted Buddha was already complete, except for one foot, which remained unpainted.
Thereupon, the bird’s tracks were left upon it as it departed. He immediately hung the scroll at Tonghwa Temple.
Whenever there were floods, droughts, epidemics, or pestilence, they invariably prayed to this Buddha, and the divine efficacy was as if miraculous.
When the state was in chaos during the Ren year, the Japanese pirates stole it away. Songyun requested its return on this account, but in the end, he did not obtain it (along with the *Xunwu zhi*).

After the Great Master himself had withdrawn into seclusion at Haein-sa on Mount Gaya following the Japanese invasion, on the twenty-third day of the first month of the Gapa year (1464), he learned that the Dharma Master Seosan had passed away.
He hurried to the capital, arriving at Yanggeum-ŭnbun Station in Gyonggun to attend the funeral.
There, he was summoned by imperial decree; unable to submit a formal memorial, he traveled by relay carriage to the capital. [The Emperor] and [the officials] above and below...

The Imperial Edict stated: "I address you, my minister: those Japanese pirates are mad; they are our sworn enemies. For six years now, the dust of war has risen and the myriad people have suffered in grief and pain.
My heart finds no peace. You shall go to see the Japanese chieftain to investigate the enemy's intentions in detail, and then return to establish friendly relations.
The Grand Preceptor bowed and withdrew from the presence, immediately preparing his travel gear. It was the spring of that year.

The journey commenced on the fourth day of the third month. Fully equipped with ceremonial regalia, incantations, and travel provisions, the protocols for their reception followed exactly the precedents set by previous envoys.
On the twentieth day, they reached Dongnae; there, they awaited a favorable wind to board ships and cross the sea.
Departing from Tsushima Island, they sailed further out to sea, arriving at the capital of Japan after several months. The Japanese received them with a grand display of ceremony.
Thirty *li* from the capital, they had set up curtains of brocade and embroidery, with gold and silver screens standing in rows on both sides.
Upon these screens were inscribed all the poems composed by the people of Japan. As the Great Master passed along the road, he glanced at them and memorized every poem.
Upon arriving at the guest house, he discussed the quality of poetry in their country with the Japanese reception officials, and was able to [cite them] immediately.
He recited the poems from behind the screen without a single error. The messenger was struck with wonder and reported this to his king.
Desiring to test his spiritual arts, the king dug a pit over ten *zhang* deep and placed a venomous snake inside.
He covered it with glass so that the snake’s form was fully exposed, appearing as if it were writhing in flowing water.
The face [of the statue] was so terrifying that it made people shudder. He invited the Great Master to enter and sit;
the Great Master also suspected it might be water, but after tossing his prayer beads, he realized they were glass and only then sat down. The Japanese ruler was increasingly impressed by his wisdom.

The following morning, as they were about to have an audience with the Japanese King, the King had iron horses set up to form a path, with glowing charcoal fires burning on all sides beneath them. He...
The Great Master entered [the hall] by way of an iron horse. The Master then turned westward and prayed in silence.

Amidst the clear blue sky and bright sun, a fragment of cloud arose from the direction of Korea, and a heavy rain immediately fell; the charcoal fires were all extinguished. Those among the Japanese sovereign and his ministers who witnessed this—

Everyone was struck with awe and said, "This is a divine monk; he is a living Buddha. They immediately carried him into the inner court on a high-quality golden palanquin and hosted a grand banquet, serving him with the reverence due to a teacher.
Whatever he said, they all followed. The Great Master then used the pretext of traveling through various provinces and states to appreciate the scenery of the mountains and rivers.
He journeyed throughout the realm of Wa, thoroughly investigating the local customs, resources, and the hearts and minds of the people. Upon his arrival...
In the fourth month of the year Wǔsì (475), as I was about to return, the King of Wa and his ministers, high and low, each presented goods and treasures as parting gifts.
The Great Master declined them all and would not accept them. First, he spoke of the matter of establishing peace and securing the nation, seeking the head of Kōsei;
next, he addressed the repatriation of the people of our country who had been captured. The King of Wa was struck with awe and immediately ordered their repatriation.
Those who had been captured since the Ren and Gui years numbered more than three thousand men and women in total.

He provided boats and provisions to escort them back, returning to the capital on the thirteenth day of the seventh month with solemn reverence. The Emperor bestowed great praise and rewards, specifically granting him the rank of First Class.
The Great Master, having no choice, entered to express his gratitude for the imperial decree and remained there for three days.
He requested to return home. It is recorded that he entered Gaya Mountain (according to the records of Sengjuhui).

In the spring of the Jiachen year, a Japanese man named Tachibana Chisei arrived and earnestly requested the transmission of news. The Master commanded the monk Wuzheng, who was in charge of general affairs, to go to Japan to investigate the situation of the invaders in detail.
Zheng crossed the sea under the pretext of traveling through various countries to enjoy the scenery of the mountains and rivers.
The Japanese found him increasingly extraordinary and invited him in a palanquin almost every day.
Upon arriving in Osaka, he first spoke of the matter of establishing peace with Ningguo, and next addressed the proposal for the repatriation of our people.

Tokugawa Ieyasu remarked, "Regarding the壬辰 (Bingchen) campaign, I truly did not witness it myself. If the two nations can remain without conflict and abide in peaceful tranquility, would that not be acceptable?"
He immediately ordered that the people who had been captured be released and sent back with them. However, at a critical juncture, he acted with deceit and craftiness, saying privately:
"Although our country and Japan have been enemies for ten thousand generations whose enmity shall never be forgotten, we have never failed in our covenant of neighborly relations.
What does a single Japanese person have to do with victory or defeat? Once the troops have withdrawn—"
Did you plot the murder of the envoys traveling between us? In the [blank] month of that year, the Yao Chieftain returned from the Central Plains;
our country received him as before. On the [blank] day of the same month, we escorted him to Busan. Now several years have passed, yet Japan holds this against us.
This must surely be a deliberate concealment intended to open a rift; otherwise, how could they blame us for a small boat crossing the vast blue sea?
"There must indeed be the peril of being adrift and drowning. The Japanese leaders and others still believed this to be true;
they spoke no further of essential matters and did not return. In the fourth month of the year *Yǐsī* (1475), Wéizhèng was about to return.

Prior to his departure, he first investigated the situation of Japan and submitted a detailed report to the imperial court, while also requesting that on the day of his return, the naval commanders and generals should be ordered to assemble and station themselves at Pusan.

"To augment the military appearance and ensure the strict protection of the various Japanese who are being escorted... [etc. On this day, the Commander-in-Chief Yi Gyeong-jeon led the naval forces toward Pusan;
however, due to unfavorable winds, they failed to arrive in time and ultimately missed the scheduled date for the expedition.

As for the three thousand or so people who had been held captive, Yi Jung returned them to Yi Gyeong-jeon, instructing him to send them back by convenient means as he saw fit. Yi Gyeong-jeon... [etc.]

Jùn assigned the boatmen to carry out their wishes. The boatmen took advantage of the situation, vying with one another to be first or last, binding and tethering them more ruthlessly than mere plunderers.
When questioned about those they were holding, they could not answer; instead, they all claimed them as their own slaves.
As for beautiful women, they would bind their husbands and throw them into the sea, taking the women for themselves as property. It was thus.
The grievances were not few, and the sound of resentment spread abroad. Heaven is high, yet its hearing is near; thus, Li Qingjun was dismissed and replaced by Li Yunlong.
Consequently, the Water Commissioners (Suisi) of each province were ordered to investigate and expose the arbitrary conduct of frontier generals.

However, the Water Commissioners treated the matter as mere formalities and ultimately failed to report it, claiming that [the situation] had improved. (Recorded by the Jinshi Zhao Qingnan following the chaos.)
With his bottle and staff in the empty mountains, he was as desolate as a withered tree or cold ashes—how still he was!
One day, rising with staff and sword, he hacked at bandits like hemp stalks—how brave he was! I do not believe that the followers of the Buddha possess substance without utility.
(Composed by Zhao Xianming, on the occasion of Zhenyuan’s true portrait.)
The monk Wijing was about to repair Longqi Mountain City when he worried that his private resources were insufficient.
He requested that the Circuit Inspector (Cuxianshi) of the province provide assistance as needed and seek out seed-grain for him.
Wijing led more than a hundred of his troops to station on the mountain slopes to cultivate fields, establishing a granary for the accumulation of grain (*Chengbi Lu*).
In the fifth month, the monk Songyun returned from Japan, escorting more than one thousand people who had been abducted back to China.
They were divided onto forty or fifty ships and returned together with the Japanese man Tachibana Tomomasa. Songyun, whose other name was Wijeong, was surnamed Yi and was a native of Milyang.
His ancestors were members of the scholar-official class (*sijuk*), though Songyun himself entered the monastic order as a monk.
He was quite capable in poetry and excelled in both regular and cursive calligraphy, gaining renown within the monastic community.

In the *Renchen* year (1212), while residing at Mount Geumgang, Japanese troops suddenly invaded one day. The temple monks fled in all directions, but Songun alone remained seated in meditation, unmoving.
The Japanese found this extraordinary; they stood around him with palms joined in respect and departed. That autumn, I was in Anju, corresponding with various provinces regardless of their status.
He urged the monastics and the laity to raise an army to support the King. When the decree arrived, Songun unfurled the document upon his meditation seat and led his followers in weeping.
He subsequently gathered over a thousand monk-soldiers and entered Pyeongrang, where they formed an array at Imwonpyeong and engaged the Japanese in successive battles.
From that time on, he remained constantly within the military ranks; furthermore, he once again entered the camp of Yi Gwang-gyeong (Cheng Zheng) to engage him in discussion. His intention was—

His spirit was fierce and fearless, such that no one could intimidate him. Last year, the court commissioned him to go to Japan under the pretext of traveling to visit mountains, in order to scout for news from within [the enemy].

Everyone considered this perilous, yet Songyun remained composed and showed no sign of distress. It was only after he had successfully returned that [the mission was deemed successful] (from the *Xiya ji*).
The head seat Hwaranwŏl was skilled in various other matters;
he was also profound in literary composition, and his collected works were circulated among the scholarly community. He once compiled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of海东* (Haidong).
At that time, Li Dongguan Yunfu said: "There was a silent practitioner whose lineage and clan were unknown. He was about fifty years old;

at times he was a shaven-headed monk, and at times a *dhūta* ascetic. He did not recite sutras nor prostrate to the Buddha, but sat in meditation all day long with his eyes closed as if in deep sleep."

There were those who observed him; regardless of their rank, from noble to humble, they could not help but change their gaze upon seeing him. When asked his name, he did not respond; when asked where he had come from, he likewise did not respond.
Thus, he was known by the name "The Silent Practitioner" (Mohe Xingzhe). He resided in a separate quarter of Guizheng Temple.
At that time, I happened to be in Kŭich’ŏng. The practitioner Chŏnch’un said to me:

“This practitioner once spent several winter months using only a single sitting mat and wearing a single patched robe (*kaṣāya*). Within his robes there were no lice or nits. Sitting upon a bed of ice, he showed no signs of cold.
When those who had recently entered the study of the Way came to him with their books to inquire about points of doubt, he would explain them to them in exhaustive detail. Just as...

During the Great Cold season, fearing that [the furnace] might freeze over, he would wait for the time when the sun came out and dispatch his disciples to quickly burn wood at the top of the hearth to warm its interior before departing.

When passersby came to look, he showed no sign of joy or resentment; he slowly stepped out of the door, gathered stones and pebbles to fill the mouth of the hearth, and plastered the crevices with mud and ash.
Then he sat in meditation as before. From then on, he never again sent anyone to warm it.
He occasionally observed fasts, eating only vegetables without sauce, yet he did not prohibit himself from eating after noon; he would eat whenever the opportunity arose.
At other times, he would go without food for seven or eight days. He said of himself that there was no mountain famous for sacred traces where he had not traveled to visit and observe.
When I went to see him previously, he did not exchange a single word with me. Later, in the tenth month of winter in the year of Yi-chou (1465), I visited Kugam-sa Temple.
A monk of the temple said, "Recently, a silent practitioner came up to Jeon-am Rock; finding it delightful, he constructed a small hermitage within a stone cave."

He personally carried stones to level the steps and newly opened a flight of stairs from the foot of the mountain to the cave, establishing more than three hundred tiers without a single stone being displaced.
At times, he would hear the signal drum for the midday meal and descend to eat; after ten or so days had passed without him returning, [the master] went to visit him.
Upon a fragment of rock was an inscribed seven-character verse composed by the practitioner. Its words were as follows: [Insert the verse here]
He was somewhat involved in the affairs of the immortals (*siddha*). In the year Gengwu, he traveled again to Kŭich’ŏng by imperial carriage along the military routes of the administrative divisions.
He asked the local practitioners where they were currently residing. The city folk replied, "Recently, they went to live in a mountain cave at Sangaeksan Gate in Chǒngju.
Last summer, they stayed at Chigwallyam Temple. At that time, they said to the temple monks: 'There is one who longs for [the north] from the north...'"
They were just now gathering at this city. Consequently, he descended the mountain and entered the city, mounted the walls to patrol, and then departed.
All the people of the city saw him. Afterwards, there appeared ghostly fires that remained hidden by day and rose up at dusk; they were blue in color and varied in size.

Sometimes they entered people’s houses, sometimes they gathered among the trees in gardens, and sometimes they flew through the air. The people of the city beat gongs and sounded whistles to drive them away.
He remained awake through the night without sleeping, continuing in this manner for several days before finally ceasing. At that time, my wife and children were residing in this city;

when I questioned them, they confirmed it was indeed so. Later, a monk named Yifēn came to inform me that he had recently gone to Sanjiǎoshān and found that the practitioner was free from ailment and doing well.
Nearby villagers, fearing the practitioner’s departure, joined together in their cultivation [of merit].

Her dwelling was a thatched hut which she tended and protected day and night. As she was about to bid farewell, the practitioner said to Fen, "Generally speaking, those who practice cultivation do not allow cold or heat to alter their resolve.

Yet the current practitioners of the Way insist on having high towers and towering halls to shelter their followers, fine food and delicate clothing to provide for their own bodies, and frequenting the company of high officials and scholars."
He exhorted him that building a temple for the sake of profit would bring greater merit than slaughtering commoners;
where, then, is the practice of a practitioner to be found? "Exert yourself and do not be negligent," he said. Bin took these words to heart.

According to the *Dongguan* (Eastern Gaze), it was for this reason that he composed this biography to supplement the omissions in the history of the monastic community (*Sengshi*). (From the *Bukan ji*)
In the tenth year of King Seongdeok’s reign, the nun Geum-gye (the wife of Tae-bu Gogdan Geum Yu-sin) issued this decree:
"Now that both the inner and outer realms are at peace, we may rest our heads high without anxiety. Great Tae-bu Gogdan..."
This is a gift from you. As a lady, you have provided mutual encouragement and support through your constant vigilance; your hidden merits are many.
I have never forgotten this in my heart and wish to repay it. I have decreed that, for one year, she shall be granted a grant of one thousand *shí* of grain from Nancheng.
Furthermore, I have commanded that Jin be tonsured as a nun and bestowed the title of Lady (*furen*).

The poet-monk State Preceptor Daegak once read the collected works of Duke Munryeol. Upon seeing the Stele Inscription for State Preceptor Daegak, it was recorded that the Master sought to leave the household life as a prince. As it says: [text continues].
Song Wendo received the dharma-gates of the five schools—Xianshou, Daxian, Tiantai, Cien, and Nanshan.
Upon reaching Sishang, he paid homage at the Śāṅgha Stūpa; at Tianzhu Temple, he paid homage to the Avalokiteśvara image, and both emitted radiant light.
Emperor Tianyou of Northern Liao heard of his reputation and sent him the Tripitaka along with six thousand nine hundred commentaries and sub-commentaries from the various schools.
In other volumes [it is recorded that] the Dharma Master Yúnxǔ of Yānjīng and the Ācārya Śīlabhadra of the Kingdom of Gaochang also both sent inquiries using written tablets and monastic robes.
All those from Liao who came on diplomatic missions were invited for an audience. When my envoys entered Liao, they likewise presented these items.
He would invariably inquire after the Master’s well-being. When the Japanese sought the Master’s epitaph and biography, they treated him with such reverence as a figure from a foreign land.
Beyond his primary studies, the Master explored the classics, histories, and the "Hundred Masters" (the various philosophical schools) to their very foundations.
Whenever he took up his pen, his prose was plain yet imbued with flavor. I requested several of his poems to taste them; Wen Liefeng’s assessment was indeed correct.
How true are the words of Dan! Upon arriving at the abbot’s quarters of Feilai (Flying Arrival), I paid my respects to the Holy Master Pude, saying:

"The teachings of the *Nirvāṇa* and the Vaipulya (*Fangdeng*) were transmitted from our own teacher. On those days when the two sages [Wonhyo and Uisang] held their scriptures side by side, they were the peerless high monks of their time.
Following conditions as they arose, they traveled freely north and south; while on the Way, they neither welcomed nor followed. You may borrow the space behind the Feilou (Flying Room)."

The ancient kingdom of Dongmyeong was in peril. (According to the Master’s own record, the Sramana Ipyeong of P’alng-sa in Goguryeo traveled to Mount Go in isolated Baekje. Later, a divine being appeared at Malyeong in Goguryeo.)
He told a person: "There will be no day when your country does not suffer defeat. Inscription on Jinseokam Hermitage: Old moss patterns like brocade; auspicious rocks stand like screens.
From time to time a high monk leans against them, Sleeping long to nourish his spiritual nature. Inscription on Yongamwon Temple: Treading through withered flowers, I ascend the verdant heights.
Pacing back and forth, gazing at the scenery, I wish to forget my return. If in years to come I am able to fulfill my former vows, I shall lie here in lofty repose.
Fog and mist set him apart from the world (*Buxian ji*).
National Preceptor Wu’ai-zhi:
beyond receiving the precepts and expounding the Way, he moved with ease through literary composition. The Wise Prince invited him into the Great [Monastery].
Inside, he earnestly entreated him to remain. The Master composed a poem, saying: The imperial decree is stern and clear; I cannot yet take my leave.
The crag-dwelling monkeys and private cranes part from Jiangdong. For many years I have fortunately avoided the fish’s baited hook; In a single day, I have instead become a bird in a cage.

They both answered with words of arrogance. Thereupon, the Emperor ordered that Renze and the others be bound and brought before the military tribunal for interrogation.
Renze, Xi, Gu, Qian, Xing, Yuanyong, Ming, Yuqing, Ren, and Ji were flogged and exiled to the southern frontiers, where they were reduced to state slaves.
He confiscated his family’s property and further exiled Xu Chengshun and Lin to the frontier. Later, when Renze heard that Ren-tun intended to kill him, he fled.

Ren-tun then had the wife and children of Renze imprisoned by the military police (*xunjun*), and furthermore, because Yu Tiangui—who served as the Director of the Office of the Household (*Sipukse*)—had once raised Renze’s younger son, he suspected him of conspiring with Renze and subjected him to severe torture.
Xin died in prison. Hui obtained the favor of being spared from the executioner’s staff as a border guard.

At first, Hui was respected by the king for his monastic conduct; however, once he married the daughter of Jinlan and kept countless concubines, he would secretly summon and take advantage of any high official’s wife who possessed a beautiful appearance. Consequently, all those in the court sought his favor and feared him.
Wei [the Prince] vied with others to present him with slaves and precious vessels. Yet the King still declined to accept his emoluments, did not approach women, and did not acquire fields or gardens;

he held him in profound trust. Wei then exercised his power and influence at will, seeking retribution for both kindness and enmity without fail. The great families and noble lineages were nearly exterminated by him;
people viewed him as a tiger or a wolf, to the point that officials had to stand guard at his residence at night. Appointments to office were granted based solely on his personal favor.

When he went out, the attendants from the rank of Palace Attendant (shìzhōng) downward escorted him before and behind, such that the roads were completely blocked and the markets could not open their goods for trade.
Qi Xian and Cui Siyuan served as his confidants, while Li Chunfu and Jin Lan acted as his wings.

His faction filled the court, and Wang also felt a sense of unease; though he held the title of "Presiding Minister" (lǐngxiāng), he did not dare to hold an official post, knowing full well [the danger].
His arrogance grew exceedingly great; fearing that the King would resent him, he subsequently plotted treason.

When the King visited the tombs of Emperors Xian and Jing, [Liu] Tui dispatched his followers to set ambushes by the roadside, intending to carry out a major act of violence upon the King’s return to the palace.

Upon the King’s arrival, Tui said to his followers, "Why did you not follow our agreement? His followers replied, "We saw that Your Majesty’s ceremonial escort was so magnificent that we could not bear to violate it."
Chen Shoufeng became enraged and cursed them, saying, "You lot are truly cowards and useless.

From then on, they gathered day and night to plot, further setting a date for the uprising. Chen Shoufeng’s guest, Li Ren, a Counselor of the Ministry of Personnel, was fully aware of this sinister scheme.
The registers of the underworld recorded this matter. As the situation became urgent, he concealed his name and styled himself the "Hermit of the Cold Forest" (*Śītavana-vāsī*).
He sent a letter by night to the residence of the Chancellor, Jin Xumìng, and immediately departed in humble attire. Xumìng reported the contents of the letter to the King.

He ordered the Imperial Guard (Seungwi-bu) to arrest Yi Hun and his faction. He had Yi Hyeon-si, Yeo Jeong-chae, Han Jin-han, Chen Yun-jian, Qi Zhongxiu, Han Yi-song, Gao Renyou, and Ju investigated them.
King Wang initially suspected that Yi Hun was being falsely implicated and did not believe the charges;
however, when his interrogated faction members all confessed, Yi Hun was exiled and his associates were subsequently executed. The King sighed and said, "Yi Ikji once said, 'Hun...'"
Those who are not upright individuals will inevitably bring about future calamities; such foresight as this is truly beyond compare.
Your servants have examined that for a sovereign governing a state, nothing takes precedence over detesting slanderers and distancing flatterers.
That these two will prove detrimental to the ancestral altars and the state is something witnessed and known by all who possess ears and eyes—namely, Zheng Shi-yun and Li Cheng-qing.
He once harbored the desire to kill him. The King urged him to go into hiding, yet Li Jixian, Li Renfu, and Han Xiu also declared that he was no upright man.
The King alone remained deluded and failed to awaken; he listened without discernment, employed him without doubt, and entrusted him with ever greater authority.
By trusting slanderous traitors and nurturing bandits, how could he possibly avoid biting his own heel in the end? One sees much of this in that king.
...this was their delusion.

The two government offices, the Censorate, and the Remonstrance Bureau submitted a memorial stating: "Great treachery is something that all under heaven and for ten thousand generations cannot tolerate.

Sin Hun was originally but a lowly monk who unwarrantedly received the sovereign's favor; his rank reached that of the highest minister, yet he presided over the advancement and dismissal of the officials."

He directed his breath as if commanding spirits, observing whether those around him were loyal to him or not, and then granting or revoking their status at will. He widely recruited bandits, coveting what was not his due.
Fortunately, by the spiritual power of our ancestors and the prescient insight of Your Highness, his secret plots were exposed;
he was dealt with according to lenient statutes and merely exiled. While the Three Han regions lost hope, the followers of Ch’ŏn—how could they possibly have harbored any other thought?
There were only seven individuals, including Yon, Ki, and Hyeon. We humbly entreat Your Highness to decide with great righteousness:
to impose the ultimate punishment upon Hyeon-gyun, to confiscate his family property, and to exterminate his faction, thereby satisfying the hearts of the masses.

The King followed this advice and dispatched the Grand Master of Ceremonies, Im Bok, and the State Councilor, Kim Du, to execute Hyeon-gyun at Suwon. Previously, the King had been in consultation with Hyeon-gyun, Chun, Pu, and others.

Ch’ung-hun said with joy, “He is summoning me back today; this makes me think of Aji even more. *Aji* is a local dialect term for a young child.

He was then executed and dismembered; his head was displayed on a pole as a warning throughout the capital.

Because Hui was by nature fearful of dogs and loathed hunting, he moreover indulged in debauchery, frequently killing black chickens and white horses to bolster his yang-qi. People of the time called Hui an "old fox-spirit."
The Kingdom of Goryeo has existed for nearly five hundred years. Heaven’s favor has already grown weary;
thus, they produced King Gongmin, who was mediocre, ignorant, and perverse, and further produced Sin Ung, who was treacherous, wicked, and rebellious.
Since the King fundamentally believed in Buddhism, Ung discoursed on emptiness to flatter him. Once the King’s dreams were deluded, Ung practiced artifice and ornamentation to curry his favor.

Once he had attained his ambitions, he sought to consolidate his favor and manipulate power. He disregarded the distinctions between superior and subordinate and destroyed the integrity of the relationship between sovereign and minister.

His attire, vehicles, and ceremonial retinue were identical to those of the sovereign. High officials, dukes, and grandees all emerged from his faction. As his following grew ever more numerous, [the situation became increasingly precarious].
To secretly plot against the proper order is a matter of the greatest gravity throughout all time and across the world; it is something that Heaven and Earth cannot tolerate.
Who is this man? His crimes and rebelliousness have reached such an extreme, yet Heaven has not swiftly punished and destroyed him, allowing him to remain until this day—what logic is there in this?
If Heaven were to look with favor upon Goryeo, supporting and securing its safety, then even if...

Because there was this treacherous and rebellious Ch’oe Ŭn, it was possible for Chong Se-woon to kill him, Yi Chun-u to dismiss him, and Yi Ch’i-hyon to expel him; otherwise, how could he have carried out his wicked schemes?
It was precisely because of Ch’oe Ŭn’s existence and the presence of King Kongmin that Ch’oe Ŭn’s descendants were able to usurp the ancestral altars and the state of King Kongmin.
Gongmin ultimately became the ruler of a fallen state. Alas! Benevolence and love are the will of Heaven toward a sovereign;
yet that which is inconstant and difficult to trust is likewise the mandate of Heaven. Heaven’s regard for Goryeo was not lacking, even unto its very lips.
Yet King Gongmin failed to revere Heaven and provoked its wrath, thereby severing his own connection with Heaven.
This is why the mandate of Heaven is not constant and is sometimes difficult to trust. How can one simply attribute this to fate?
Let future rulers not fail to realize that the sovereign mandate is not easily maintained; let the reign of King Gongmin serve as a solemn warning.
